articles.title: SJAA EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document is the "SJAA EPHEMERIS," Volume 3, Number 9, serving as the official publication for the San Jose Astronomical Association. Published in September 1992, it likely functioned as a newsletter or periodical disseminating information relevant to the association's members during that month.

articles.title: The EYEPIECE
articles.summary: This editorial reflects on a summer of excellent observations and encourages members to share their experiences. It highlights an upcoming Peace Corps mission for Del Johnson, who plans to promote amateur astronomy abroad with a small telescope, and mentions a recent successful Yosemite star party. The article also provides a detailed calendar of upcoming club events, including star parties, astronomy classes, and general meetings for September and October.

articles.title: News Flash!
articles.summary: Jim Van Nuland announced the birth of his new grandson, Erik Johathon Van Nuland, playfully referred to as a "double star" or "double discovery." The report notes that Jim, the new grandmother, and all involved are doing well.

articles.title: Astronomy Magazine Renewal Time
articles.summary: SJAA is organizing group renewals for Astronomy magazine subscriptions through Jim Van Nuland. Current SJAA subscribers will be contacted with pricing (tentatively $14), while new subscribers and independent subscribers expiring in 1993 can inquire to join the group rate. Members are explicitly warned not to send payment directly to the magazine, as the group rate offers significant savings.

articles.title: Special Notice
articles.summary: The September beginning astronomy class has been rescheduled to September 11, instead of September 19, due to the Milpitas Library room being unavailable for that date this month only. The document also lists the current officers of the organization, including the President, Vice President, Treasurer, Secretary, and Editors.

articles.title: Arcane Equations Led Einstein and All of Us Into a Relative World. His Theories Upset Newton's and Now Have Survived a Series of Tough Tests Trains, Lighting and Space
articles.summary: Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity, developed in 1915, revolutionized physics by accurately predicting Mercury's orbital changes and superseding Newton's laws of motion and gravity. This enduring theory has survived numerous rigorous tests, forming the basis of modern physics with practical applications in space exploration and astrophysics. Its profound impact also influenced 20th-century thought by challenging absolute concepts of time and space and made Einstein a public figure.

articles.title: Testing for Ether
articles.summary: The article discusses the historical context and implications of the Michelson-Morley experiment, which failed to detect the existence of a stationary 'ether' thought to fill space. It then explains how Albert Einstein's 1905 Special Theory of Relativity provided the answer, positing that the speed of light is constant in all frames of reference and abandoning notions of absolute time and motion. This new theory, which included the famous E=mc² equation, resolved paradoxes in Newtonian physics and eliminated the need for the ether.

articles.title: The Acceleration Problem
articles.summary: This article introduces "The Acceleration Problem" that Einstein faced in expanding his theory of relativity. While uniform motion is relative, acceleration appears to be absolute, leading to a contradiction where the laws of nature would seem different for varying states of motion. Einstein sought a unified physics conformable to a general principle of relativity, regardless of a body's state of motion.

articles.title: Fremont Peak B-B-Q and Star Party by Paul Barton
articles.summary: The Fremont Peak B-B-Q and Star Party, a joint event by FPOA and SJAA, was an exceptionally well-attended and organized outing, described as the best of the year. Over a hundred people enjoyed a vast array of telescopes, abundant food, social interaction, and exceptional viewing conditions with warm, clear, and dew-free skies. Highlights included the 30" Challenger telescope, a T-scanner for solar prominences, and the gracious hospitality of Ranger Rick Morales.

articles.title: Henry Coe Star Party by Paul Barton
articles.summary: This article reports on the Henry Coe Star Party, highlighting an outstanding outing characterized by warm, dry weather, good sky conditions with fog below, and a strong turnout of attendees and their telescopes. Participants enjoyed observing until moonrise, with particular praise for Alan Nelms' stable and optically fine 9-inch Takahasi telescope. The report concludes with a reminder about checking the area for lost items and trash to ensure continued access for future events.

articles.title: Houge Park - 7 Aug. 1992 by Paul Barton
articles.summary: Paul Barton's report details a well-attended public star party at Houge Park on August 7, 1992, featuring 15+ telescopes and 50-100 visitors. Attendees observed various celestial objects including the Moon, Saturn, several nebulae and clusters, Uranus, and Neptune, though the bright moon obscured the Perseid meteors. The event highlighted strong community support, the involvement of an astronomy class, and included a personal announcement regarding a member's family.

articles.title: Double, Triple, and Multiple Stars
articles.summary: This article by Patrick M. Donnelly provides a personal list of ten excellent double stars for observing during September evenings. The selection criteria prioritize visibility, ease of resolution, brightness, and color contrast, making them enjoyable for amateur astronomers. The list includes stars like Gamma Andromedae and Beta Cygni (Alberio), detailing their magnitudes and separations.

articles.title: COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: This article reports on the recovery of three faint periodic comets—Giclas (1992 I), Wolf (1992m), and Schuster (1992n)—all recovered by T. Seki, noting their current magnitudes and projected brightness at perihelion. Meanwhile, Comets Shoemaker-Levy and Machholtz are fading from view, leading to an expectation of low comet activity for the upcoming months unless a new bright comet is discovered.

Ads are accepted by the 12th of each month and run for approximately three months. For each celestial body, it lists its distance in Astronomical Units (A.U.), apparent magnitude, and three time entries likely representing rise, transit, and set times. This data serves as a guide for astronomical observers interested in these objects.

This information serves as a practical reference for planning astronomical observations.
